I’m thinking of replying and telling her I have 'personal reasons' to decline, because declining feels like a clean break, whereas failing after accepting feels like a death sentence to my career.
sandhi_response: Saying no before you can be tested feels like a shield against the pain of potentially falling short of your own high standards. But you were chosen because of your potential to learn, not because you already have all the answers, and you deserve to take this step.

user_input: I got a 5-star rating on my mock placement interview yesterday, and the training cell officer told me I’m a shoo-in for the Tier-1 companies coming next week. Instead of feeling motivated, I’ve spent the last 24 hours locked in my hostel room feeling utterly sick. If I actually get a 20+ LPA offer, it means I have to pack up, move to Bangalore, survive the corporate grind, and handle absolute independence when I can barely handle my own laundry right now. I’m literally considering skipping the placement drives and settling for some local mass recruiter because the thought of actually succeeding and having to step up to that life is making me physically vomit.
sandhi_response: The transition that success demands can feel like an overwhelming leap into a life you don't feel ready to manage yet. It is entirely okay to feel terrified of the future, but remember you only have to take it day by day, not solve your entire adult life in a single weekend.

user_input: I actually cleared the round-3 coding assessment for that crazy 24 LPA tech giant, and instead of being happy, my stomach is in knots. I keep hoping they'll reject me in the final HR round because if I actually get this job, everyone will realize I just googled my way through DSA and can't code to save my life. If I fail now, it's fine, but if I succeed and then get fired for being useless, I won't survive the shame.
sandhi_response: It makes complete sense that this sudden leap feels terrifying, as if stepping into success is just setting you up for a steeper fall. You do not have to carry the weight of an entire career today, so try to take things one step at a time.

user_input: My professor wants to nominate me as the student lead for our department's upcoming national hackathon because of my past project. I literally want to decline it and make up some family emergency to get out of it. If I say yes, I'm signing up for a massive spotlight where every single mistake I make will be blown up, and everyone will see I'm just a mediocre coder who got lucky once.
sandhi_response: Stepping into the spotlight can feel like placing a target on your back, making safety seem like it only exists in staying small. But you did not trick anyone into seeing your value, and it is safe for you to occupy this space and learn as you go.

user_input: I somehow got a perfect 10 CGPA this semester, and honestly, I wish I got an 8.5 instead. Now my parents are bragging to every relative on WhatsApp, and my professors are expecting me to lead the department research project next term. The pressure is suffocating me because I know I can't maintain this, and the drop from the top is going to hurt so much worse.
sandhi_response: Reaching the top should not feel like a trap where your only reward is a heavier burden of expectations. Your worth is not a high-wire act you have to perform perfectly forever, and you are allowed to just be a student who did well.

user_input: My professor nominated me for the fully-funded summer internship in Germany, and I’m genuinely thinking of rejecting it. My friends have been struggling with backlogs and bad grades, and if I take this, I know it's going to create this weird, silent wall between us. I'd rather stay back with them and be normal than be successful and completely isolated.
sandhi_response: It is incredibly painful to feel like your growth might cost you the connections that keep you safe and grounded. Your success does not mean you are leaving others behind, and you deserve to see how far you can fly without holding yourself back.

user_input: I'm in the final round for a huge consulting firm next week. Last night, I literally sat down and thought about intentionally bombing the case study round just to get it over with. If I actually get the offer, I'll have to move to a new city, work 80 hours a week, and prove myself all over again, and I don't think I have the stamina to keep up with who they think I am.
sandhi_response: The fear of what success will demand of you can make self-sabotage feel like the only way to protect your peace. It is okay to take a deep breath and realize you do not have to conquer all of tomorrow's demands today.

user_input: I somehow cleared the second round of the Amazon interview today. Instead of feeling happy, my stomach is in knots. I literally looked at the confirmation email and felt this overwhelming urge to just ghost them. If I get this job, my parents are going to tell the whole neighborhood, and then I’m stuck. Every single day will be a fight to prove I’m not a fraud who just memorized three trees-and-graphs templates on LeetCode. It feels safer to just fail the next round and blame it on hard questions so everyone stops expecting me to be some coding genius.
sandhi_response: It is incredibly heavy to feel like your achievements are just traps setting you up for a bigger fall. You don't have to carry the weight of everyone's future expectations right now; you are allowed to just take this one interview step-by-step, simply as a curious learner.

user_input: My professor wants to publish my DBMS project paper in an international journal and nominated me as the lead student researcher. I’ve been ignoring his emails for four days now. I keep thinking, if I say yes, I’m locking myself into this identity of a high-achiever, and I cannot keep up with that. My friends are already teasing me about getting a 'fat package' and calling me the department topper, and it makes me want to crawl into a hole. I’m seriously considering copying someone else's minor assignment just so the prof thinks I'm mediocre and leaves me alone.
sandhi_response: It makes complete sense that you want to shrink back when success feels like a contract that strips away your right to be ordinary or make mistakes. Your worth isn't tied to being a perpetual high-achiever, and you deserve to explore your capabilities without the suffocating weight of everyone's spotlight.

user_input: I just got my 5th semester SGPA back and it's a 9.4. I should be celebrating, but honestly? I felt this cold wave of dread. The first thing I thought was, 'Now I have to maintain this.' If I drop to an 8.5 next semester, it's going to look like a massive failure compared to this, and my relatives will have a field day talking about my 'downfall.' Part of me wishes I had just got an average 7.5 so I could breathe without feeling like I'm standing on the edge of a cliff waiting to be pushed off.
sandhi_response: Earning a high grade should feel like a victory, yet it feels like you've just been placed on a higher pedestal where the wind is much colder. Please remember that a single semester's score is just a snapshot of a moment, not a lifetime promise of perfection you are obligated to keep.

user_input: Our team won the college hackathon, and they want me to present our prototype to some venture capitalists coming to campus next week. I literally told my team members to take my name off the slide and let someone else do it. Every time I think about presenting, I picture them asking deep technical questions and realizing I don't actually understand the system architecture as well as my teammates. If I do well, I’ll be expected to lead the next startup incubator phase, and I just want to hide in my room and play games. I hate that I'm sabotaging my own career, but the safety of being a nobody feels so much better than the terror of being noticed.
sandhi_response: Stepping into the spotlight is terrifying when it feels like a setup for public exposure rather than a celebration of your hard work. You don't have to be a flawless expert to share what you built; you are allowed to occupy space and own your contribution, even while still figuring things out.

user_input: I got shortlisted for the final HR round of a dream product company. It pays more than double what my dad makes. But instead of studying, I spent the last two days binge-watching sitcoms and eating instant noodles. I feel this weird, heavy resistance to opening my laptop. It’s like, if I actually land this job, my whole life changes, and the expectations from my family will become unbearable—they’ll expect me to buy a house, support my cousins, and never have a weak moment. If I just mess up the HR round by giving bad answers, I can go back to being the 'struggling student' where nothing is expected of me.
sandhi_response: It is incredibly exhausting when a professional milestone feels like an anchor of familial duty before you've even had a chance to celebrate it. Your career is allowed to be just yours—a path for your own growth and security—rather than an immediate solution to everyone else's struggles.
